title: Evaluating Creativity in Large Language Models
abs: Large language models have demonstrated an increasing ability to generate diverse and novel content, raising questions about whether their outputs can be considered creative. This work presents a systematic evaluation framework for measuring creativity in LLM-generated text. We evaluate models across divergent thinking, storytelling, analogy generation, and alternative-use tasks using metrics for novelty, diversity, coherence, and usefulness. Our results show that modern LLMs can produce highly fluent and diverse responses, but their performance varies substantially across creativity dimensions. In particular, models tend to achieve high scores in elaboration and fluency while struggling with originality when prompts closely resemble patterns observed during training.
body:
Creativity is commonly characterized by the ability to generate ideas that are both novel and useful. Recent advances in large language models have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generating stories, solving open-ended problems, and proposing novel ideas. However, evaluating creativity in these systems remains challenging because conventional language-model benchmarks primarily focus on correctness rather than novelty.

In this work, we develop a multi-dimensional framework for evaluating creativity in LLMs. Our framework considers fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration, and usefulness. We construct a benchmark containing open-ended tasks from divergent thinking, storytelling, analogy generation, and problem-solving domains.

We evaluate several contemporary language models under different prompting strategies. The results indicate that prompting substantially influences creative performance. Models generally generate fluent and well-structured responses, but many responses remain semantically close to common solutions. Increasing sampling diversity improves originality but can negatively affect coherence. These findings suggest that creativity in LLMs is not a single capability and requires evaluation across multiple complementary dimensions.

title: Self-Consistency Improves Reasoning in Large Language Models
abs: Chain-of-thought prompting has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, individual reasoning trajectories can contain errors that propagate to the final answer. We investigate self-consistency, an approach that samples multiple reasoning paths and aggregates their final answers. Experiments across arithmetic, symbolic reasoning, and commonsense benchmarks show that self-consistency can significantly improve accuracy without modifying model parameters. Our analysis further demonstrates that diverse reasoning trajectories provide a useful source of robustness, although the computational cost grows with the number of sampled responses.
body:
Large language models frequently produce correct answers to reasoning problems, but their performance can be sensitive to the particular reasoning trajectory generated during inference. A model may follow one reasoning path that leads to an incorrect conclusion despite having sufficient knowledge to solve the problem correctly.

We investigate whether sampling multiple independent reasoning trajectories can improve reliability. Given an input question, the model generates several solutions using stochastic decoding. Instead of selecting the first response, we aggregate the resulting answers and choose the most frequently occurring solution.

We evaluate this strategy on mathematical reasoning, symbolic manipulation, and commonsense reasoning tasks. Across all evaluated domains, self-consistency improves performance compared with single-sample chain-of-thought prompting. The largest improvements occur on problems where multiple valid reasoning paths exist. However, additional samples provide diminishing returns, indicating a trade-off between computational cost and accuracy.

title: Understanding Representation Collapse in Language Models
abs: Representation collapse refers to a phenomenon in which diverse inputs are mapped to increasingly similar representations. While representation geometry has been extensively studied in vision models, its role in large language models remains less understood. We analyze hidden states across multiple transformer layers and investigate how semantic diversity, token diversity, and task diversity affect representation structure. Our experiments reveal that different layers exhibit distinct geometric regimes, with intermediate representations preserving substantially more diversity than final-layer representations. We further show that excessive concentration of representations can negatively affect generation diversity.
body:
Transformer language models transform sequences of discrete tokens into high-dimensional continuous representations. These representations encode linguistic, semantic, and contextual information and provide the foundation for downstream prediction.

An important question is how the geometry of this representation space changes during training and inference. In particular, we study whether representations of semantically different inputs become increasingly concentrated in a limited region of the latent space.

We collect hidden states from multiple transformer layers across diverse datasets and measure representation diversity using cosine similarity, covariance statistics, effective rank, and entropy-based metrics. Our experiments show that representation geometry changes considerably across layers. Early layers preserve lexical information, while intermediate layers exhibit stronger semantic organization. Later layers become increasingly specialized for next-token prediction.

We observe that models with lower representation diversity tend to produce less diverse outputs under comparable decoding settings. These observations motivate further investigation into the relationship between latent-space geometry and generative diversity.

title: Test-Time Compute for Improving Large Language Model Reasoning
abs: Increasing inference-time computation has emerged as an effective approach for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Rather than relying on a single forward generation, test-time computation allows models to generate, evaluate, refine, or combine multiple candidate solutions. This paper studies several inference-time strategies, including best-of-N sampling, self-reflection, answer aggregation, and verifier-guided search. Results across mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that additional inference computation can substantially improve performance, particularly when models are capable of identifying and correcting their own errors.
body:
Scaling language models has traditionally focused on increasing the number of parameters and the amount of training data. More recently, researchers have investigated whether computation performed after training can also improve model capabilities.

We study test-time computation as a general framework for allocating additional computation to difficult inputs. Instead of producing a single response, a model can generate multiple candidate solutions and use an evaluator to select the most promising candidate. More sophisticated approaches allow the model to iteratively critique and revise its responses.

We compare four strategies: independent sampling, best-of-N selection, self-refinement, and verifier-guided search. Experiments show that increasing the number of candidate solutions generally improves accuracy, although the improvement depends strongly on the quality of the evaluator. Self-refinement is particularly effective when the model can reliably identify errors in intermediate reasoning.

These findings suggest that inference-time scaling provides an alternative axis for improving language-model performance and may be particularly valuable for computationally demanding reasoning tasks.

title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models
abs: Large language models can generate fluent and plausible statements that are unsupported by available evidence. These hallucinations limit the reliability of LLMs in knowledge-intensive applications. We introduce a framework for measuring hallucination across factual question answering, summarization, and long-form generation. The framework separates factual correctness, evidence attribution, and uncertainty calibration. Our experiments demonstrate that conventional accuracy metrics can substantially underestimate hallucination rates, particularly for open-ended generation.
body:
Hallucination is one of the major challenges facing the deployment of large language models. A response may be linguistically coherent and internally consistent while containing claims that cannot be supported by reliable evidence.

Existing evaluation methods often treat hallucination as a binary factuality problem. However, factual reliability has several dimensions. A model may provide a correct statement without citing evidence, provide an incorrect statement with high confidence, or combine several correct facts into an unsupported conclusion.

We therefore introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework based on factual correctness, source attribution, and confidence calibration. We evaluate several language models across question answering and summarization tasks.

Our analysis shows that models with similar benchmark accuracy can exhibit substantially different hallucination behavior. Retrieval augmentation reduces unsupported factual claims in many settings, but does not eliminate hallucinations entirely.

title: Can Large Language Models Generate Novel Scientific Hypotheses?
abs: Large language models are increasingly being explored as assistants for scientific discovery. This study investigates whether LLMs can generate hypotheses that are both novel and scientifically plausible. We develop a benchmark based on scientific literature and evaluate generated hypotheses according to novelty, relevance, plausibility, and testability. The results indicate that LLMs can produce hypotheses that combine concepts from different areas of knowledge, but many generated ideas remain close to existing literature. Retrieval and structured prompting improve factual grounding while sometimes reducing novelty.
body:
Scientific discovery often requires combining existing knowledge in ways that produce new and testable hypotheses. The broad knowledge encoded by large language models makes them promising tools for assisting this process.

We investigate the hypothesis-generation capabilities of language models across several scientific domains. Models are asked to propose research questions and hypotheses based on a collection of scientific concepts. Generated ideas are evaluated using both automated similarity measures and expert assessment.

Our results reveal a trade-off between novelty and grounding. Models provided with extensive literature context generate more scientifically plausible ideas, but their proposals tend to remain closer to existing work. In contrast, models operating with less contextual information generate more unusual hypotheses but also produce a larger number of implausible claims.

These findings suggest that LLMs may be most effective as collaborative scientific tools, where researchers use model-generated hypotheses as starting points for exploration rather than treating them as autonomous discoveries.
